# The Problem with Financial Systems: An Overview — Bangalore, April 2018

**Date:** April 10, 2018  
**Location:** IBM Office, Bangalore, India  
**Type:** Recorded working session — informal teaching and group discussion  
**Facilitator:** Kip M. Twitchell  
**Participants:** IBM engineers and staff, Bangalore office  
**Video:** [Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PjzfaxvQ9WQ) (56:56)  
**Published:** December 17, 2019 (unpublished episode of *Conversations with Kip*)  
**Status:** Raw auto-generated transcript. Not formal minutes.

---

## Context

This session was an informal presentation and group discussion given by Kip Twitchell to a room of IBM engineers in Bangalore. It was not originally intended as a Sharealedger meeting — it was a spontaneous teaching session on a trip. But the content makes it one of the most complete single-session articulations of the core financial systems problem that Sharealedger exists to address.

The audience is smart but not financial-systems-specialist. That's the strength of the session: Kip builds the entire argument from personal spending data upward — no assumed knowledge, genuine questions from the room, real Socratic dialogue. By the end, the case for why financial systems are architecturally broken — and why now is the moment to fix them — is fully made.

**Key ideas developed in this session:**

- Every person's lifetime purchase history (~1.3 million line items) could, in principle, produce any financial report, forecast, or risk analysis on demand — the way Dr. William McCarthy proposed in 1982
- We don't do this because financial systems were built when compute and storage were expensive; the architecture was designed to *throw away transactions and keep only balances*
- Balances are duplicates of transactions — they reduce response time but create an explosion of reconciliation cost that *cannot be fully automated*
- The same constraint that justified this architecture in the 1970s (cost) has been eliminated by 50 years of Moore's Law; the architecture has not changed
- "Running the computer backwards" — when a balance is wrong, analysts manually dump data to Excel and re-add rows to find the detail; this happens everywhere, every day, and likely represents 30% of financial services operating costs

This is the problem Sharealedger is organized to solve.
